subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Reading the Story Aloud

time_bands.activity: The teacher shows the chapter title and the illustration on the opening page (Textbook pp. 9–13). Ask students: 'What do you think tinkling bells are? Who might want them?'

Teacher reads the entire narrative aloud expressively (Textbook pp. 9–13), pausing briefly at Chinna losing his money, at Kamala's advice, and at the fruit-seller scene to let students absorb the emotional turns.

Shared reading: students follow along silently while the teacher re-reads pp. 9–13 one section at a time. At each natural pause, the teacher asks a quick oral check — 'Who is Tara?' 'What did Chinna see at Chacha's shop?' — to confirm comprehension without formal questioning.
Students take turns reading aloud in pairs — one reads a paragraph, the other listens and corrects mispronunciations gently. Teacher circulates and provides pronunciation support.
Class shares one word each that stayed with them from the story (e.g., 'tinkling', 'honest', 'dejected'). Teacher notes the words briefly on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage benefit greatly from a rich first encounter with the text before any task is attempted; resist the urge to ask comprehension questions during the read-aloud. Watch for children who struggle to decode 'dejected' and 'pineapple' — model the syllable breaks clearly during the shared-reading phase.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.14): answer four short-answer questions about Chinna's story.
Let us Think — B. (p.14): write T or F for five statements about the narrative.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the four questions in Let us Think A aloud (Textbook p. 14) one by one, giving students a moment to locate the relevant part of the story each time.

Let us Think — A. (p.14): students answer the four short-answer questions independently in their exercise books. Teacher circulates and prompts those who are stuck with a page hint — 'Check the paragraph where Chinna gets home' — rather than giving the answer.

Let us Think — B. (p.14): teacher reads each True/False statement aloud; students write T or F and underline the sentence in the story that proves their choice. Discuss each verdict as a class, accepting only story-based justifications.

Whole-class verification: three students share their answer to Question A4 (how Chinna managed to buy the bells). Teacher guides a brief discussion on why Kamala's words about empathy mattered, drawing directly from the narrative.
Students read back one of their own written answers to a partner and together decide if it is complete. Teacher listens in and gives brief oral feedback to a few pairs.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly confuse the sequence of events — particularly placing the fruit-seller scene before or after Kamala's market trip. Encourage them to skim-read the story one more time before writing. The True/False task works best when students are held to finding textual evidence; accept no guesses without a story reference.

periods.activity_title: Listen, Sequence, Then Speak — Story Order and Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.18): listen to the story, then number six sentences in correct story sequence.
Let us Think — C. (p.14): think-and-discuss why Chinna returned the extra money.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the full narrative 'The Tinkling Bells' aloud at a measured pace (Textbook p. 18 transcript reference). Students listen with books closed.
Teacher reads the story aloud a second time while students mentally track the sequence of events. No writing yet — purely attentive listening.

Let us Listen (p.18): teacher distributes or writes the six sequencing sentences on the board. Students number them in the order the events occurred in the story, working individually, then compare with a neighbour.
Class reviews the correct sequence together. Teacher calls on students to say, in a complete sentence, what happens at each step — building oral retelling alongside verification.

Let us Think — C. (p.14): guided discussion in pairs, then whole class — 'Why do you think Chinna decided to return the money instead of keeping it?' Teacher elicits story-based reasoning (Kamala's empathy reminder) before accepting personal values.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening-and-sequence task requires the teacher to read at a deliberately unhurried pace so that students can track events; two readings are the minimum for this age group before independent sequencing. Students who confuse steps 3 and 4 (mother's promise vs. market trip) likely need one more slow read-aloud of that passage — offer it quietly to the group rather than singling individuals out.

periods.activity_title: What Would You Do? — Ethical Dilemma Speaking

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (pp.18–19): discuss four ethical situation prompts aloud in pairs and with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the moment Chinna whispered to his mother about keeping the extra money, and the moment he ran back to return it. Ask the class: 'Has there ever been a moment when you had to make a hard choice?' Warm up the room for values talk.

Let us Speak (pp.18–19): teacher reads the four ethical situation prompts one by one. For each, students first think silently for thirty seconds, then discuss in pairs. Teacher circulates and listens without correcting moral positions — only scaffolding language ('Can you say more? What happened next?').

Whole-class share-out: one pair presents their response to each situation. Classmates may agree, disagree, or add to any response. Teacher guides the conversation to stay grounded in reasons, not just 'I would do the right thing'.
Quick round: each student finishes the sentence 'Being honest means…' aloud in one sentence. Teacher listens and affirms diverse, genuine responses without ranking them.

periods.teacher_notes: The four dilemmas — the broken pen, the math-quiz temptation, the classmate's theft, and the snack-sharing scenario — escalate in social difficulty; start with the broken-pen prompt to ease the class in. Students sometimes give the 'approved' answer without reasoning; press gently with 'Why?' or 'What would happen if everyone did that?' to develop genuine ethical thinking rather than rehearsed responses.

periods.activity_title: Words of Value — Word Search and Opposites

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.15): find ten value-related words in the word-search grid.
Let us Learn — C. (pp.17–18): circle the opposite of each highlighted story word.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the ten target words (CALM, HONEST, LOVE, RESPECT, COURAGE, LOYAL, TRUTH, FAIR, KIND, PEACE) on the board and reads them aloud with the class. Students say a quick meaning they know for at least three words before opening the textbook.

Let us Learn — A. (p.15): students work on the word-search grid individually. Teacher sets an informal challenge — find at least six before checking with a partner. After searching, pairs confirm each other's circled words.

Class verification: teacher calls out each word in turn; students say where they found it (across, down, diagonal). Briefly discuss one word's meaning from the story context — 'Chinna showed HONESTY when he returned the money.'

Let us Learn — C. (pp.17–18): teacher reads each sentence aloud, students decide which option is the opposite of the highlighted word and circle it. After completing all four, pairs compare and justify their choices using the story's own context.
Rapid oral round: teacher says a word from the task (e.g., 'beautiful', 'reward', 'buy', 'whispered') and students call out its opposite. Reinforce by placing the word in a sentence from the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse 'antonym' tasks with 'similar meaning' tasks — for item C1, watch for students choosing 'Attractive' (which means the same as 'beautiful') rather than 'Ugly'. Ground each opposite choice firmly in the story context: Chinna's bells were 'beautiful', not 'ugly', and that contrast is exactly what the task asks students to identify.
materials: Pencils or coloured pencils for the word search

periods.activity_title: Degrees of Comparison — Grammar in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.16–17): study comparative adjective forms with Chinna, Charu, Jasmine; fill in five blanks with -er or -est.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws three stick figures on the board labelled Chinna, Charu, Jasmine and introduces the idea: 'Chinna is tall. Charu is taller. Jasmine is the tallest.' Students look at the textbook illustrations on p. 16 and repeat each sentence chorally, feeling the -er and -est endings.

Teacher reads aloud the grammar rule box on p. 16 with students following. Three more pairs of sentences from everyday classroom life are modelled — 'This pencil is long. That ruler is longer. The table is the longest.' Students suggest their own examples before moving to the textbook task.

Let us Learn — B. (p.17): students complete the five fill-in blanks independently. Teacher circulates; for students who are stuck, prompt with 'Are we comparing two things or the whole group?' rather than giving the answer.
Class correction: each blank is verified aloud. A student explains why -er or -est was chosen for each item. Teacher corrects gently where the reason is missing or confused.
Quick pair challenge: each student makes up one original comparison sentence about someone in the classroom — 'My bag is heavier than Riya's bag' — and shares it aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often overgeneralise and write 'tallest than' instead of 'taller than' — emphasise that 'than' always goes with -er (two things), and 'the' always introduces -est (the whole group). The three-figure visual on p. 16 is the key anchor; keep returning students to it whenever they confuse the forms.

periods.activity_title: Story Words in New Sentences — Guided Sentence Framing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (pp.19–20): frame original sentences using five story words: smiling, mistake, honest, praise, careful.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five words on the board: smiling, mistake, honest, praise, careful. For each, the teacher and class together recall how it was used in the story — 'Kamala was smiling when Chinna returned the extra money.' This warm-up grounds the vocabulary before independent writing.

Modelled writing: teacher thinks aloud and writes one complete sample sentence for 'smiling' — 'The teacher was smiling when all the students completed their homework on time.' Students observe the full sentence structure (subject + verb + context) before attempting their own.

Let us Write — A. (pp.19–20): students write their own original sentence for each of the five words independently. Encourage sentences that go beyond the story — personal experience, classroom life — as long as the word is used correctly. Teacher circulates, noting common errors in word order or tense for whole-class feedback.

Peer response: students exchange books with a partner and check that each sentence (a) contains the target word, (b) makes sense, and (c) has a capital letter and full stop. Partners put a tick and, if needed, suggest one small fix.
Two or three students share their favourite sentence aloud. Teacher praises specific qualities — 'I like that you used 'honest' in a situation from your own life.'

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently copy the story's own sentence when framing; gently redirect them: 'Can you write about your own life using this word?' Watch especially for 'smiling' being misused as a noun ('I saw a smiling') — model the -ing form as a describing word within a full clause. The peer-check step builds reading and editing habits simultaneously.

periods.activity_title: Bells Around Us — Craft, Puzzle, and Picture Collection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (pp.20–22): make a tinkling bell craft from recyclable materials provided in class.
Let us Explore (p.23): draw or describe different types of bells found in India.

homework.task_brief: Fun with Matchsticks (p.23): solve the matchstick equation puzzle by moving one matchstick to make the equation correct.

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up the textbook illustration of the tinkling bells (pp. 9–10) and asks: 'Where else do we see or hear bells in India?' Students call out examples — temple bells, school bells, cowbells, cycle bells, doorbells — building background for the exploration task.

Let us Do (pp.20–22): teacher distributes materials (small bottle caps, string, pebbles, aluminium foil, cardboard tags, markers) and walks the class through the craft steps together. Students assemble their own tinkling bell, decorate a cardboard tag with their name or a drawing, and attach it to the string. Teacher assists with the hole-punch or nail step.

Students shake their finished bells and the class enjoys the sound together. Each student gives their bell a name and shares it in one sentence — 'My bell is called Peace Bell because it sounds calm.'

Let us Explore (p.23): students draw at least two types of bells found in India (e.g., temple bell, school bell, cowbell, bicycle bell) in their exercise book and write one sentence about each — what it looks like and where it is used.

Gallery moment: students hold up their bell crafts and drawings for the class to see. Teacher connects back to the story: 'Chinna wanted these bells because he loved Tara — what does your bell mean to you?'

periods.teacher_notes: Gather the craft materials (bottle caps, string, small pebbles, foil, markers) before the sitting; the assembly works best when all items are laid out on desks before students arrive. Students who finish the craft quickly can begin the bell-drawing task early. The matchstick puzzle is set as homework because it benefits from unhurried individual puzzling, and the visual is best attempted with the textbook in hand at p. 23.
materials: Small metal bottle caps or small tin cans (cleaned)

items.item_stem: Read these statements about 'The Tinkling Bells' and write True or False for each one.

options.text: Chinna decided to keep the extra money and asked his mother to stay quiet about it.
Chinna found his money missing when he tried to buy the bells at Chacha's shop.
Kamala scolded Chinna angrily when he came home feeling sad about his lost money.
The fruit seller gave Chinna ten rupees extra by mistake while returning change.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — Chinna discovered his money was missing at the shop. 2. False — Kamala comforted him gently and promised to give him money. 3. True — the pineapple seller accidentally gave ten rupees extra. 4. False — Chinna was moved by Kamala's words and ran back to return the money.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves and verifies story events using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Chinna's lost money, Kamala's comfort, fruit-seller's extra change, return of money, buying the bells.
items.item_stem: Kamala told Chinna that keeping the extra money would be the same as stealing. She reminded him of something he had felt himself that very day. What did she remind him of, and why do you think those words made Chinna run back to the fruit seller?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Kamala reminded Chinna how sad and helpless he himself had felt when his own money went missing. Hearing this, Chinna understood that the fruit seller would feel the same loss, and so he ran back and returned the extra ten rupees.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the story 'The Tinkling Bells' aloud. Listen carefully and then arrange these events in the order they happen in the story by writing numbers 1 to 6.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Event | Order |
|---|---|
| Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller. | |
| Chinna and his mother went to the market together. | |
| Chinna saw the tinkling bells at Chacha's shop and wanted to buy them. | |
| Chinna told his mother about the missing money and she comforted him. | |
| The fruit seller accidentally gave Chinna ten rupees extra as change. | |
| Chinna bought the tinkling bells and tied them around Tara's neck. | |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: See answer_key for the correct order.

answer_key.left: Chinna saw the tinkling bells at Chacha's shop and wanted to buy them.
Chinna told his mother about the missing money and she comforted him.
Chinna and his mother went to the market together.
The fruit seller accidentally gave Chinna ten rupees extra as change.
Chinna returned the extra money to the fruit seller.
Chinna bought the tinkling bells and tied them around Tara's neck.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Chinna standing at the fruit stall with ten extra rupees in your hand. Your teacher will ask you to speak aloud: What are you thinking at that moment? What do you finally decide to do, and why?

expected_elements: Names the temptation to keep the money.
Links the decision to empathy or honesty.
States the action taken and a reason.

|---|---|
| Temple bell | On a bicycle in the street |
| School bell | At a place of worship |
| Cycle bell | Around a cow or goat's neck |
| Cowbell | Telling students a class has ended |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Temple bell–at a place of worship; School bell–telling students a class has ended; Cycle bell–on a bicycle in the street; Cowbell–around a cow or goat's neck.

items.item_stem: In the story, Chinna made his pet goat Tara happy by tying tinkling bells around her neck. Think about a bell you have seen or heard in your life. Tell your teacher: What does the bell look like? Where have you seen or heard it? Why is that bell special or important to you?

expected_elements: Names or describes a specific bell observed.
States where or when the bell is used.
